    How the scales work
    Every component is 0 to 100 on an absolute scale, so a house scored today compares to one scored in March. These are the anchors, and they are the only place they are written down: the cards print facts, not scales.
    Condition
    The cost-weighted share of this house's possible work that is NOT expected, from the cost model's own probabilities. 100 means nothing is expected; 0 means every line lands. Mechanicals are aged, so a component at the end of its life counts more. Nobody has stood in any of these houses, so photographs alone cannot take a house much above 80.
    Space
    0 below 1,300 sq ft above grade, most of the points by 1,700, the rest to 2,600. A finished basement adds 3 of 25, a separate entrance 2.
    Layout
    Bedrooms carry 80 of 100, a primary over 150 sq ft adds 10, an ensuite adds 10, and any bedroom under 100 sq ft costs 20. The ensuite is read from the room table where there is one and inferred from the bath count where there is not; the card says which.
    Baths
    One full bath scores 25, two 65, three 90, four or more 100, and a powder room adds 10. Counts only; nothing here is about condition.
    Location
    Five parts out of 100. Commute 30: 0 at 6 km from the nearest GO station, 100 at 1.5 km. Quiet 20: 0 within 200 m of the QEW, 403, 407 or the rail corridor, 100 beyond 600 m, with a bonus for a court or crescent and a cap for a named arterial. Walk and transit 25: 0 at 45 between them, 100 at 120. School 15: 0 with none within 1.0 km, 100 within 0.5 km. Green and water 10: 0 beyond 2 km from the shore and every park over 5 ha, 100 within 500 m of either.
    Lot
    3,000 sq ft scores 0 and 7,000 scores 100, straight line between. Your numbers for small and plenty.
    Parking
    Each garage space counts 3 and each driveway spot 1, capped at 8, so 8 or more scores 100.
    Price (the cost side)
    No penalty at or under $6,000 a month, your comfortable payment, rising in a straight line to the full penalty at $7,000, your maximum. Above the maximum it holds at the full penalty. At the dial the page is set to, the full penalty costs 18 quality points.
    Quality
    The seven things that are not price, each 0 to 100 on an absolute scale, combined with the current weights. Higher is better. It says how good the house is, and says nothing about what it costs.
    Cost, and the dial
    Price is not one of the seven. It is a penalty in quality points: nothing at or under your comfortable payment, rising to the full penalty at your maximum. The dial is how many quality points that full penalty is worth, and the list is sorted on quality minus the dial's share of it. At a dial of 0 the list is quality only. The dial is provisional, like the weights: it is set so that price counts exactly as much as its provisional weight says.
    Condition
    The share of this house's work that is not expected, cost-weighted, 0 to 100. The dollars behind it are under Renovations. A clean read lowers a job's odds to a floor of 15%, never to zero, so photographs alone cannot push it past 80; the rest needs somebody standing in the house.
    Monthly payment
    Mortgage principal and interest at the settings in the control bar, plus property tax, plus upkeep. The only number on this page with "/mo" after it, and every place it appears it is the same figure.
    Day-one work
    The 80th percentile of what must be done before or at move-in: safety, insurability, and work that costs twice as much once the furniture is in.
    Wish list
    Kitchen, baths, basement, deck. Your choice, your timing. It is priced but it never gates a purchase.
    5-year cost
    What owning for the hold costs beyond getting the price back: financing and opportunity cost, commission out, land transfer tax, closing, unrecovered day-one work, tax and upkeep. A total, never a monthly figure, because it is not a payment.
    Cash on closing day
    Down payment, land transfer tax net of the first-time-buyer rebate, closing extras and day-one work. What has to be in the account.
    Band
    Where this house lands across every weight set on file, every hold of 3, 5 and 10 years, and the low and high end of its own day-one uncertainty. A wide band means the rank is resting on assumptions.
    Project
    Expected work is more than 15% of the asking price. Ranked, not excluded, because you said you would take one on at the right price.
    HOLD
    An oil tank, an in-ground pool or a sitting tenant. Ranked and flagged, never silently dropped, and never marked "See first".
    Weights
    What each component is worth, out of 100. The weights on this page are provisional: a starting order proposed on 13 September (condition, space, price, layout, baths, location, lot, parking), not one either of you set. The order at the top of the list holds up well if they change; the middle of the list is where they matter.

    How the order works. Four steps, and no step knows about the next one.
    1. Rules first, before any scoring. A house that fails one is not ranked: confirmed basement moisture, fewer bedrooms above grade than you set, over a budget or cash ceiling if you set one, or a project if you had said no projects. 0 of 39 fail one. They sit at the end with the reason on the card.
    2. Seven things about the house, each out of 100. Space, layout, baths, parking, lot, location and condition. Every one is an absolute scale, so a house scored today is comparable to one scored in March, and none of them moves when the batch changes. Together, weighted, they are quality.
    3. The weights. Provisional: a starting order, not one either of you set. The top of the list holds up if they change; the middle is where they matter.
    4. One score, sorted descending. Quality, docked 5% for a split-level plan, less what the monthly payment takes off above your comfortable $6,000 a month. That is the whole rule. The band beside it is where the house lands across every hold and the two ends of its own day-one uncertainty.
    One rule underneath all of it: photographs can only ever count against a house, except through condition, where a clean full-resolution read can lower a finish line toward a floor of 15%, never to zero, and a clean read never deletes a job either. No photograph moves a roof or a furnace. Photographs alone cannot push condition past 80 of 100; the rest needs somebody standing in the house.

Kitchen and bath figures come from published Ontario contractor ranges. The rest are working estimates and are the first thing to replace with a real quote.

                                                                                      Per year includes HST. This is the honest cost of owning a house with mechanical equipment in it, whether or not anything breaks in your first year. Because only four of the 37 listings showed anything mechanical (a tankless water heater at Barberry, a tank at Pallatine, a furnace cabinet at Samford, PEX lines at Kent) and none showed a panel, every house here is charged the full reserve. One date from the agent removes most of it: a 2023 furnace drops that line to near zero for a decade.

                                                                                      A job you cannot see is priced at the odds it has never been done, set by the age of the house. Reading the sink rim, the counter edge, the soffit and the door profile at full resolution pulls that number down toward 15%. Seeing a defect pins it at 100%. That is the whole mechanism, and it is why the houses whose tells came back original carry the largest wish lists.

                                                                                      Appraisal Institute of Canada bands, with the bathroom low end pulled down to match the RE/MAX renovation report. Almost nothing returns more than it costs. Spending past what a renovated house in that pocket sells for returns 45 cents on the dollar, which is the arithmetic behind the old rule about not over-improving for the street.

                                                                                      The single most sensitive number on this page: a renovated house is assumed to trade at $720 per usable sq ft in Burlington and $790 in Oakville. Both are derived from asking prices, not sold prices. Move them by $60 and several of the resale figures move by six digits. Ask the agent for sold price per square foot in each pocket, and this stops being a guess.

                                                                                      Two questions that go to every listing agent, always

                                                                                      1. How old are the roof, furnace and air conditioner?
                                                                                      2. Are any of the photos virtually staged or digitally enhanced, and when were they taken?

                                                                                      Not one of these 37 listings contains a photograph of an electrical panel, and only four show any mechanical equipment at all. Across houses built between 1950 and 2008, that is the largest gap in everything above, and the first question closes most of it. Two listings were caught overstating: Oxlow calls an above-ground pool in-ground, and Tania has at least one virtually staged basement frame.

                                                                                      This cannot tell you a house is good

                                                                                      It is a screening tool and a list of things to check. Every green line means "no problem found in the photos", never "verified fine".

                                                                                      None of these are offer prices

                                                                                      There are no sold comparables in this model. Resale estimates rest on an asking-price benchmark and will move the moment real sold data exists.

                                                                                      The calculator is arithmetic, not advice

                                                                                      Rates, insurance premiums and rebate rules change. Confirm every figure with your mortgage broker and your real estate lawyer before you rely on it.

                                                                                      It knows nothing about living there

                                                                                      The street, the light, the noise, the walk to the car in February. All of it outranks everything on this page.

                                                                                      Where your gut and the model disagree

                                                                                      One dot per house per person: the gut score you gave it against the score the model gives it. It appears once five gut scores exist, and it is the mechanism that replaces redesigns with weight edits.

                                                                                      One score out of 100: quality from seven components on absolute scales, weighted by provisional weights, less a cost penalty on the monthly payment between $6,000 and $7,000 · condition is the cost-weighted share of this house's work that is not expected, two-sided at full resolution, capped for photographs; a clean read lowers a job to a floor, never deletes it · cost of capital 4.0%, derived from 4.25% on 80% and 3.0% on the down payment · exit commission 5.5% · no appreciation assumed · Model v3.5, rank v6.2, 25 September 2026 · 39 listings, all photo-graded · Nothing here is an offer price
